lines.text: Twenty times a number is a perfect square. Fifty times the same number is a perfect cube.
lines.caption: Twenty times a number is a perfect square. Fifty times the same number is a perfect cube.

lines.text: Can one small number do both jobs? <short pause> It can, and we'll find it two ways.
lines.caption: Can one small number do both jobs? It can, and we'll find it two ways.

lines.text: Hi there, I'm Vantee! Let's crack this one together.
lines.caption: Hi there, I'm Vantee! Let's crack this one together.

lines.text: Here's the question.
lines.caption: Here's the question.

lines.text: What is the smallest positive integer n, such that twenty times n is a perfect square,
lines.caption: What is the smallest positive integer n, such that twenty times n is a perfect square,

lines.text: and fifty times n is a perfect cube?
lines.caption: and fifty times n is a perfect cube?

lines.text: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
lines.caption: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

lines.text: Let's break it down. A perfect square is a whole number times itself, like nine, or four hundred.
lines.caption: Let's break it down. A perfect square is a whole number times itself, like nine, or four hundred.

lines.text: A perfect cube is a whole number times itself, times itself again, like eight, or one thousand.
lines.caption: A perfect cube is a whole number times itself, times itself again, like eight, or one thousand.

lines.text: We need ONE number n that does both jobs. And we want the smallest one!
lines.caption: We need ONE number n that does both jobs. And we want the smallest one!

lines.text: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
lines.caption: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

lines.text: Welcome back! Let's start with the square part, and make a list.
lines.caption: Welcome back! Let's start with the square part, and make a list.

lines.text: Twenty is four times five, and four is already a perfect square.
lines.caption: Twenty is four times five, and four is already a perfect square.

lines.text: So twenty times n is a square exactly when five times n is a square.
lines.caption: So twenty times n is a square exactly when five times n is a square.

lines.text: For that, the five needs a partner five. So n is five times a perfect square.
lines.caption: For that, the five needs a partner five. So n is five times a perfect square.

lines.text: That gives five, twenty, forty-five, eighty, and so on, smallest first.
lines.caption: That gives five, twenty, forty-five, eighty, and so on, smallest first.

lines.text: Now the cube test. Start with n equals five. Fifty times five is two hundred fifty.
lines.caption: Now the cube test. Start with n equals five. Fifty times five is two hundred fifty.

lines.text: Six cubed is two hundred sixteen. Seven cubed is three hundred forty-three.
lines.caption: Six cubed is two hundred sixteen. Seven cubed is three hundred forty-three.

lines.text: Two hundred fifty sits in between, so it's NOT a cube.
lines.caption: Two hundred fifty sits in between, so it's NOT a cube.

lines.text: Next up, n equals twenty. Fifty times twenty is one thousand. That's ten times ten times ten!
lines.caption: Next up, n equals twenty. Fifty times twenty is one thousand. That's ten times ten times ten!

lines.text: We went smallest first, so twenty is the smallest that works. That's Choice B!
lines.caption: We went smallest first, so twenty is the smallest that works. That's Choice B!

lines.text: Here's a second way, with prime factors.
lines.caption: Here's a second way, with prime factors.

lines.text: Twenty is two times two times five. Fifty is two times five times five.
lines.caption: Twenty is two times two times five. Fifty is two times five times five.

lines.text: In a perfect square, every prime shows up an even number of times.
lines.caption: In a perfect square, every prime shows up an even number of times.

lines.text: Four hundred has four copies of two, and two copies of five. Both even!
lines.caption: Four hundred has four copies of two, and two copies of five. Both even!

lines.text: In a perfect cube, every count is a multiple of three, like one thousand: three of each.
lines.caption: In a perfect cube, every count is a multiple of three, like one thousand: three of each.

lines.text: Say n has x copies of two, and y copies of five.
lines.caption: Say n has x copies of two, and y copies of five.

lines.text: Other primes don't help the twos or the fives. They'd only make n bigger.
lines.caption: Other primes don't help the twos or the fives. They'd only make n bigger.

lines.text: First, the twos. Twenty times n has x plus two of them. Fifty times n has x plus one.
lines.caption: First, the twos. Twenty times n has x plus two of them. Fifty times n has x plus one.

lines.text: For the square, x plus two is even. So x is zero, two, four, and so on.
lines.caption: For the square, x plus two is even. So x is zero, two, four, and so on.

lines.text: For the cube, x plus one is a multiple of three. So x is two, five, eight, and so on.
lines.caption: For the cube, x plus one is a multiple of three. So x is two, five, eight, and so on.

lines.text: The smallest number on both lists is two.
lines.caption: The smallest number on both lists is two.

lines.text: Now the fives. Twenty times n has y plus one of them. Fifty times n has y plus two.
lines.caption: Now the fives. Twenty times n has y plus one of them. Fifty times n has y plus two.

lines.text: For the square, y plus one is even. So y is one, three, five, and so on.
lines.caption: For the square, y plus one is even. So y is one, three, five, and so on.

lines.text: For the cube, y plus two is a multiple of three. So y is one, four, seven, and so on.
lines.caption: For the cube, y plus two is a multiple of three. So y is one, four, seven, and so on.

lines.text: Both lists start at one! So n is two times two times five, which is twenty. Same answer!
lines.caption: Both lists start at one! So n is two times two times five, which is twenty. Same answer!

lines.text: Which way should you pick? A list is quick for small answers. Counting primes always works.
lines.caption: Which way should you pick? A list is quick for small answers. Counting primes always works.

lines.text: Now the traps. Choice D uses the number fifty itself.
lines.caption: Now the traps. Choice D uses the number fifty itself.

lines.text: Twenty times fifty is one thousand. That's a cube, but not a square.
lines.caption: Twenty times fifty is one thousand. That's a cube, but not a square.

lines.text: Fifty times fifty is a square, but not a cube. The two jobs got swapped!
lines.caption: Fifty times fifty is a square, but not a cube. The two jobs got swapped!

lines.text: Choice E is one hundred, since twenty and fifty both divide it. But two thousand isn't a square.
lines.caption: Choice E is one hundred, since twenty and fifty both divide it. But two thousand isn't a square.

lines.text: Choice A, ten, gives two hundred and then five hundred. Neither one works.
lines.caption: Choice A, ten, gives two hundred and then five hundred. Neither one works.

lines.text: Choice C, forty, gives eight hundred and then two thousand. Those fail too.
lines.caption: Choice C, forty, gives eight hundred and then two thousand. Those fail too.

lines.text: And don't stop at five! It passes the square test, but fails the cube. Always check BOTH rules.
lines.caption: And don't stop at five! It passes the square test, but fails the cube. Always check BOTH rules.

lines.text: Ready for a challenge? Find the smallest positive integer n,
lines.caption: Ready for a challenge? Find the smallest positive integer n,

lines.text: such that two times n is a perfect square, and three times n is a perfect cube.
lines.caption: such that two times n is a perfect square, and three times n is a perfect cube.

lines.text: Pause the video, and go for it!
lines.caption: Pause the video, and go for it!

lines.text: Let's count primes. Say n has x copies of two, and y copies of three.
lines.caption: Let's count primes. Say n has x copies of two, and y copies of three.

lines.text: For the twos, x plus one is even, and x is a multiple of three. So x is three.
lines.caption: For the twos, x plus one is even, and x is a multiple of three. So x is three.

lines.text: Threes: y is even, and y plus one is a multiple of three. So y is two.
lines.caption: Threes: y is even, and y plus one is a multiple of three. So y is two.

lines.text: So n is two cubed times three squared. That's eight times nine, which is seventy-two!
lines.caption: So n is two cubed times three squared. That's eight times nine, which is seventy-two!

lines.text: Check: two times seventy-two is one hundred forty-four, which is twelve times twelve.
lines.caption: Check: two times seventy-two is one hundred forty-four, which is twelve times twelve.

lines.text: And three times seventy-two is two hundred sixteen, which is six times six times six.
lines.caption: And three times seventy-two is two hundred sixteen, which is six times six times six.

lines.text: If you found seventy-two, amazing work!
lines.caption: If you found seventy-two, amazing work!

lines.text: Here's the big idea to remember.
lines.caption: Here's the big idea to remember.

lines.text: Break the number into primes, and count the copies of each prime.
lines.caption: Break the number into primes, and count the copies of each prime.

lines.text: Square: every count is even. Cube: every count is a multiple of three.
lines.caption: Square: every count is even. Cube: every count is a multiple of three.

lines.text: I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
lines.caption: I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
